reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / GOLD & ATS guidelines
clinicalPearls: Chylothorax is the accumulation of lymphatic fluid (chyle) in the pleural space due to disruption or obstruction of the thoracic duct
The aspirated fluid is classically milky and opalescent, though it may appear serous when the patient is fasting or malnourished
The diagnosis is confirmed by an elevated pleural fluid triglyceride level and, when uncertain, the demonstration of chylomicrons
Common causes are malignancy (especially lymphoma) obstructing lymphatic flow and trauma or surgery injuring the thoracic duct
Non-traumatic causes also include lymphangioleiomyomatosis, cirrhosis, and central venous thrombosis
Persistent drainage of chyle leads to loss of protein, fat, fat-soluble vitamins, and lymphocytes, causing malnutrition and immunosuppression
Initial management often includes drainage and a low-fat or medium-chain-triglyceride diet, or bowel rest, to reduce chyle flow
Refractory or high-output leaks may require thoracic duct ligation, embolisation, pleurodesis, or shunting
reference.pathophysiology: The thoracic duct conveys chyle, rich in triglycerides absorbed from the gut, from the abdomen to the systemic venous circulation. When the duct is disrupted by surgery or trauma, or obstructed by tumour or fibrosis, chyle leaks into or backs up into the pleural space. Because chyle contains chylomicrons and high triglyceride content, the effusion has a characteristic milky appearance and high triglyceride level. Ongoing leakage depletes the body of nutrients, immunoglobulins, and lymphocytes, and the volume loss can cause hypovolaemia and metabolic disturbance.
additionalDifferentials: Transudative effusion from heart failure or cirrhosis
additionalInvestigations: Pleural fluid triglyceride measurement and, if equivocal, lipoprotein analysis for chylomicrons
Cross-sectional imaging to identify malignancy or thoracic duct obstruction
Lymphangiography or lymphoscintigraphy to localise the site of leak in selected cases
Assessment of nutritional status and lymphocyte count with prolonged drainage
Investigation for underlying causes such as lymphoma or lymphangioleiomyomatosis
redFlags: High-output chyle leak causing rapid nutritional and immune depletion
Signs of malnutrition, hypovolaemia, or lymphopenia-related infection
Underlying malignancy such as lymphoma requiring urgent evaluation
Respiratory compromise from a large or rapidly reaccumulating effusion
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying cause and leak volume; traumatic and postsurgical chylothoraces often settle with conservative measures, whereas malignant or high-output leaks are more difficult to control and prolonged chyle loss risks serious malnutrition and immunosuppression if not addressed.
pitfalls: Assuming turbid pleural fluid is empyema without measuring triglycerides
Overlooking a false-negative milky appearance in a fasting patient
Allowing prolonged high-volume drainage without addressing nutritional and immune depletion
Failing to investigate for an underlying malignancy in non-traumatic cases
